title: Vowel Sounds: Pure Vowels and Diphthongs

blocks.text: In the Oral English paper a candidate is asked which word has the same vowel as seat. She picks sit because the letters look alike. Sit is /i/; seat is /iː/. The extra length is the whole point of the question. WAEC does not mark spelling in this section. It marks the sound you would hear if a speaker of Received Pronunciation said the word.

blocks.markdown:
English has **twelve pure vowels** (the tongue stays in one place) and **eight diphthongs** (the tongue glides from one position to another). Length is part of the identity of a pure vowel: the short set and the long set are different sounds, not the same sound stretched.

Paper 3 will not ask you to draw a vowel chart. It will give you a word with underlined letters and four options, and you must choose the option that shares that **sound**, whatever the spelling.

blocks.title: Spelling is not the sound
blocks.text: Though, through, thought, thorough and tough look like a family. They are not. Though is /ðəʊ/, through is /θruː/, thought is /θɔːt/, thorough is /ˈθʌrə/, tough is /tʌf/. Train your ear on the vowel, then confirm with a known rhyming word.

blocks.caption: The twelve pure vowels, with the pairs WAEC tests most

blocks.markdown:
### Diphthongs: a glide, not two vowels side by side

A diphthong is one syllable. The tongue starts at one position and moves toward another inside the same beat.

**Closing diphthongs** (the tongue moves toward /i/ or /ʊ/):

- /eɪ/ — *day, they, break, great, weigh*
- /aɪ/ — *buy, high, height, eye, aisle*
- /ɔɪ/ — *boy, noise, employ*
- /əʊ/ — *go, though, sew, boat, know*
- /aʊ/ — *now, bough, drought, how*

**Centring diphthongs** (the tongue moves toward /ə/):

- /ɪə/ — *here, beard, fierce, idea*
- /eə/ — *there, hair, wear, their, bear*
- /ʊə/ — *poor, tour, sure*

If you can freeze the tongue halfway, you are saying two syllables, not a diphthong. *Boy* is one glide /bɔɪ/, not *bo-ee*.

blocks.title: Grouping by sound, not spelling
blocks.prompt: Which of these words shares the vowel of GO: though, through, thought, tough?

steps.text: Say GO slowly. It is a diphthong: the tongue starts near /ə/ and glides toward /ʊ/. The symbol is /əʊ/.
though — /ðəʊ/. Same glide as go, despite the -ough spelling.
through — /θruː/. A long pure vowel /uː/, the same family as food, not go.
thought — /θɔːt/. A long pure vowel /ɔː/, the same family as caught.
tough — /tʌf/. A short pure vowel /ʌ/, the same family as cut.
Only though matches GO. The shared letters -ough are a trap.

blocks.answer: though — both words have the diphthong /əʊ/.

blocks.title: Pairs that Nigerian speakers often merge
blocks.text: /i/ and /iː/ (sit/seat), /æ/ and /ɑː/ (cat/cart), /ʌ/ and /ɒ/ (cut/cot), /ɒ/ and /ɔː/ (cot/caught), /ʊ/ and /uː/ (pull/pool). If your everyday speech does not keep a pair apart, learn one keyword for each sound and test every option against that keyword, not against your first guess.

blocks.title: WAEC Oral English tip
blocks.text: Do not look for the same letters. Look for a word you already know that rhymes with the keyword in Received Pronunciation. Seat rhymes with beat and machine, not with sit. Blood rhymes with flood, not with brood. Great rhymes with late, not with greet. If two options look equally 'close' in spelling, they are probably the trap.

points: Short and long pure vowels are different sounds: sit /i/ is not seat /iː/.
The twelve pure vowels include /æ/, /ɑː/, /ʌ/, /ɒ/, /ɔː/, /ʊ/, /uː/, /ə/ and /ɜː/.
A diphthong is a glide inside one syllable: /eɪ/ /aɪ/ /ɔɪ/ /əʊ/ /aʊ/ /ɪə/ /eə/ /ʊə/.
Words that share a spelling such as -ough do not necessarily share a vowel.
WAEC asks you to group by sound: choose the option that matches the underlined vowel, not the letters.
